text.p: Following are some of the major events to have occurred on July 30 in history.
1178 - Frederick I, Holy Roman Emperor known as Barbarossa, was crowned King of Burgundy.
1419 - Anti-Catholic Hussites, followers of executed reformer Jan Hus, stormed the town hall in Prague and threw Catholic councillors out of the windows.
1511 - Giorgi Vasari, Italian painter, architect and art historian, born.
1619 - The first legislative assembly in America, known as the House of Burgesses, was convened in Jamestown, Virginia.
1656 - Charles X of Sweden defeated the Poles at the Battle of Warsaw, two days after invading the country.
1718 - William Penn, English Quaker leader who founded the American state of Pennsylvania, died.
1771 - Thomas Gray, English poet noted for his "Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard", died.
1818 - Emily Bronte, English novelist, born. Best known for her "Wuthering Heights", she was a sister of Anne and Charlotte Bronte.
1863 - Henry Ford, founder and president of the Ford Motor Company, born.
1898 - Otto von Bismarck, founder and first chancellor of the German Empire, died.
1898 - Henry Moore, one of the best known English sculptors, born. His most notable commissions were the UNESCO building in Paris and the Lincoln Center, New York.
1909 - Professor Cyril Northcote Parkinson, who invented "Parkinson's Law", born. His law says that work expands to fill the time available for its completion.
1934 - Kurt von Schuschnigg was named Austrian chancellor following the assassination of Engelbert Dollfuss.

1935 - The first Penguin book was published, starting the paperback revolution. The idea came from Sir Allen Lane, who wanted to provide "a whole book for the price of 10 cigarettes". The first one to be issued was "Ariel" by Andre Maurois.
1941 - Paul Anka, Canadian singer and songwriter who had several hit records including "Diana" and "Puppy Love", born.
1945 - The U.S. cruiser Indianapolis was sunk by a Japanese submarine killing over 800. It was returning to the U.S. after delivering nuclear material for the atomic bomb.
1948 - The advance of Communist domination in Hungary forced the resignation of President Zoltan Tildy.
1949 - British warship HMS Amethyst made its escape down the Yangtze River, having been refused a safe passage by Chinese Communists after a three-month standoff.
1963 - Soviet newspaper Izvestia reported that Kim Philby, recently revealed as the "third man" in Britain's Burgess and Maclean spy affair, had been given asylum in Moscow.
1966 - England beat Germany 4-2 at Wembley to win the football World Cup.
1971 - During the Apollo 15 mission, David Scott and James Irwin landed on the moon.
1971 - A Japanese Boeing 727 collided with a jet fighter over Shizukuishi, killing 162 people.
1973 - The 11-year battle for the victims of the drug Thalidomide ended with compensation payments of 20 million pounds sterling.
1974 - Joint declaration on Cyprus was signed in Geneva between Greece, Turkey and Britain.
1975 - A summit conference on European security opened in Helsinki attended by leaders of 35 nations including U.S. President Ford and Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev.
1980 - The Republic of Vanuatu (formerly the Franco-British condominium of New Hebrides) achieved its independence.
1989 - General Wojciech Jaruzelski stepped down after eight years as Polish Communist Party leader. He was succeeded by his friend and protege, Mieczyslaw Rakowski.
1989 - Radical members of the Soviet parliament set up a group to press for faster reform. Boris Yeltsin and Andrei Sakharov were among those elected to run it.
1990 - British Conservative member of parliament Ian Gow, close aide of Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher, was killed by a car bomb planted by Irish republicans.
1991 - President Bush and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev began a two-day summit meeting in Moscow, Bush's first summit on Soviet soil.
1993 - In Geneva peace talks, Bosnia's Moslems, Serbs and Croats agreed to create a new "union" of three ethnic republics.
1994 - Zaire declared its eastern region, swamped by 1.7 million Rwandan refugees, a disaster region.

1996 - Claudette Colbert, queen of 1930s Hollywood comedies, died. Colbert won an Academy Award for best actress for her performance in the screwball comedy, "It Happened One Night", in 1934. She was 92.
